title: Azure Core in Plain English: Scope, Access and Guardrails
summary: Understand Azure management hierarchy, RBAC and Policy before operating cloud resources.
plain_language_explanation: Azure operations are governed by scope. Management groups organize subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups and resources, RBAC controls who can perform actions, and Azure Policy evaluates whether resource state follows organizational rules. Treat authorization and compliance as related but different controls.
quick_check: Why can a user have RBAC permission to deploy a resource and still be blocked by Azure Policy?

title: Azure Resource Hierarchy, RBAC and Policy Boundaries
summary: Design Azure scope and access so platform governance does not collapse into broad standing privilege.
objective: Explain how management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, RBAC and Policy combine into an enterprise control plane.
body_outline: Use management groups to organize and govern subscriptions; avoid mirroring every organization chart layer into the hierarchy.
Treat subscriptions as strong units of management and isolation for workloads and environments.
Assign RBAC at the lowest practical scope and distinguish control-plane authorization from data-plane permissions.
Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and actions against organizational rules; it complements rather than replaces RBAC.
Inherited RBAC and Policy assignments must be traced from parent scopes before diagnosing an unexpected allow or deny.
Separate privileged platform administration from workload-team access and use time-bound elevation where the organization supports it.

title: Azure Virtual Networks, Segmentation and NSG Control
summary: Operate Azure network boundaries by separating address design, routing and security filtering.
objective: Build a layered mental model for Azure virtual networking and traffic controls without treating an NSG as a complete network architecture.
body_outline: Azure Virtual Network is the private-network foundation for Azure resources and connectivity to other networks.
Design address spaces and subnets to support routing, segmentation and future connectivity rather than only current VM count.
NSGs filter inbound and outbound traffic using ordered rules and can apply at subnet or network-interface scope.
Use deny-by-default and permit-by-exception patterns where appropriate; avoid broad administrative exposure.
Separate routing failures from security-rule failures and from name-resolution or platform-service dependencies.
Hybrid connectivity, firewalls, DDoS controls and application-layer protections are distinct layers and should be introduced deliberately.

title: Azure Operations Control Loop: Monitor, Query, Alert and Govern
summary: Connect Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, alerts and Policy into an evidence-driven operating model.
architecture_notes: Azure operations should form a control loop: collect platform telemetry, query evidence, alert on meaningful conditions, compare resource state with policy, and route remediation through an authorized change process. Monitoring and governance are different planes: an alert reports a condition; Policy evaluates compliance or can enforce effects. Neither replaces workload-level health verification.
failure_modes: resource exists but diagnostic data is not routed where operators expect
alert rule fires but action group or incident routing is ineffective
KQL query scope omits the relevant workspace or resource
RBAC allows an operation that Policy denies
Policy compliance is green while application health is degraded
NSG change is blamed for an outage before effective routes and name resolution are checked
operators remediate policy drift without understanding exemption or change ownership
enterprise_design_notes: Use consistent diagnostic settings, workspace strategy, alert ownership, policy assignment provenance and exception governance. Production remediation should be auditable and reversible rather than triggered from an unreviewed discovery script.

title: Read-Only Azure Governance, Network and Monitoring Evidence Pack
summary: Collect Azure scope, RBAC, Policy, VNet and monitoring evidence without changing resources.
objective: Produce a timestamped Azure operations dossier before any RBAC, Policy, network or monitoring change is proposed.
steps: Record tenant and subscription context and confirm the approved scope before querying resources.
Inventory resource groups and representative resources without creating, updating or deleting anything.
List role assignments and policy assignments at the approved scope and record inherited controls separately.
Inventory virtual networks, subnets and NSGs and capture rule metadata without editing rules.
Inspect Azure Monitor alerts and Log Analytics workspace metadata without changing diagnostic settings or action groups.
Classify findings as authorization, governance, network, observability or workload-health issues before proposing remediation.
expected_result: A read-only Azure evidence pack showing scope, access, governance, network and monitoring state with no resource mutation.
rollback: Not required; the prescribed commands are read-only.

title: Azure Access, Policy, Network or Monitoring Incident Decision Tree
summary: Separate Azure authorization, governance, network and observability failure domains before changing production controls.
diagnostic_order: Confirm tenant, subscription and resource scope before interpreting any access or inventory result.
For denied operations, separate authentication, RBAC authorization, Policy deny effects and resource-provider state.
For connectivity failures, check effective addressing, routing, NSG rules, name resolution and endpoint/application health as separate layers.
For missing telemetry, prove data source, diagnostic collection path, workspace/query scope and alert rule before changing thresholds.
Preserve activity-log, alert and policy-compliance evidence before remediation.
Escalate when resolution requires privilege elevation, role changes, policy exemptions, NSG/routing changes, diagnostic-setting changes or resource restart/redeployment.
escalation_boundary: Do not add role assignments, create policy exemptions, modify NSGs/routes, enable public access, change diagnostic settings, restart resources or deploy remediation from this troubleshooting workflow without approved change authority.

title: Azure Core Operations and Governance Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering scope, RBAC, Policy, network controls and operational telemetry.

assessment_items.question: What is the key difference between Azure RBAC and Azure Policy?
assessment_items.answer: RBAC governs who can perform actions at scopes; Policy evaluates or enforces whether resource state and actions comply with organizational rules.

assessment_items.question: Why should an operator inspect inherited assignments before changing a local role or policy?
assessment_items.answer: Effective access and compliance can originate at parent scopes, so changing the child scope may not address the actual control and may weaken governance.

assessment_items.question: Does an NSG replace routing and application health checks?
assessment_items.answer: No. NSGs filter traffic, while routing, DNS, platform connectivity and the workload itself remain separate failure domains.

assessment_items.question: Why is a green Policy compliance state not proof of service health?
assessment_items.answer: Policy measures configured governance rules, not end-to-end workload availability, correctness or performance.

title: Senior Azure Interview: Governance, Networking and Operations
summary: Senior scenarios testing Azure scope design, least privilege, policy governance, network isolation and operational evidence.

questions.question: A deployment is denied although the engineer has Contributor. How do you investigate?
answer_points: separate RBAC from Azure Policy deny effects
avoid granting Owner as a diagnostic shortcut

questions.question: A VM cannot reach an internal service. What layers do you prove before editing NSGs?
answer_points: NSG rules at subnet and NIC
hybrid or firewall path if applicable

questions.question: What makes Azure monitoring operationally useful rather than merely enabled?
How would you keep workload teams autonomous without giving them platform-wide privilege?
answer_points: use subscriptions/resource groups as workload scopes
assign least-privilege RBAC lower in hierarchy
retain platform governance at management-group/subscription layers
use privileged elevation for exceptional access
